metadata.aiExecutiveSummary: Questo brief presenta una panoramica sui paper scientifici disponibili su arXiv nella categoria q-bio.NC, focalizzandosi sulle neuroscienze e la cognizione. Tali risorse spesso esplorano l'architettura neurale, i meccanismi cognitivi e le loro implicazioni, utilizzando metodologie che vanno dall'analisi teorica alla modellazione computazionale e agli studi empirici. La loro importanza risiede nel far avanzare la comprensione del cervello e della mente, contribuendo allo sviluppo di nuove teorie e applicazioni tecnologiche.
aiKeyTakeaways: Esplorare regolarmente la sezione q-bio.NC di arXiv per rimanere aggiornati sulle ultime scoperte in neuroscienze e cognizione.
Identificare studi che utilizzano metodologie innovative per affrontare sfide complesse nella comprensione del cervello e dei sistemi neurali.
Valutare l'applicabilità dei modelli computazionali e delle analisi teoriche presentate ai propri progetti di ricerca o sviluppo tecnologico.
Considerare le implicazioni etiche e filosofiche delle ricerche sulla coscienza e l'intelligenza artificiale avanzata.
Utilizzare i paper come base per approfondire le conoscenze su specifiche patologie neurologiche o funzioni cognitive.

# Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience in Continuous Substrates: A Falsifiable Programme

> **Il documento definisce un programma di ricerca falsificabile di stampo lakatosiano per identificare le condizioni fisiche necessarie per la sembianza o senzienza interocettiva primaria in substrati neuromorfi continui. Stabilisce criteri operativi di demarcazione rispetto alle architetture digitali canoniche e introduce cinque condizioni fisiche vincolanti. Il framework si articola attorno a ipotesi ausiliarie verificabili tramite protocolli preregistrati con controlli negativi espliciti.**

---

Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive
Sentience
in Continuous Substrates
A Falsifiable Programme
Francesco Iavarone
Independent Researcher
Version 0.1, revision 6 — September 2026
Abstract
We formulate necessary physical conditions for primary interoceptive sentience in continu-
ous neuromorphic substrates, and specify falsifiable tests for them. The programme does not
claim to be a theory of consciousness and does not claim that the conditions it formulates
are sufficient. Its central claim is conditional: if primary interoceptive sentience is instan-
tiated in a continuous physical substrate, then the conditions formulated here must hold.
The conditions are of two kinds: (i) three operational demarcation conditions — causal non-
separability, non-Markovian memory, state-dependent effective dynamics — that distinguish
continuous substrates from verified digital architectures without depending on contested re-
sults; (ii) five necessary physical conditions — local activity at the edge of chaos, robust
causal degeneracy, critical scale-invariance, homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability,
and an autopoietic barrier. The programme is Lakatosian: its hard core is a metaphysical
postulate (dual-aspect monism of valence), not falsifiable by the programme’s tests; its pro-
tective belt consists of seven falsifiable hypotheses; its empirical commitments are specified
in a preregistered protocol with six negative controls and five abandonment criteria. To
the best of our knowledge, no existing work combines these four elements — operational
demarcation, five necessary conditions, preregistered protocol with negative controls, and
Lakatosian framing — for primary interoceptive sentience in continuous substrates, though
the survey underlying this claim (Section 2) covers five works and two lines of research, and
is not a systematic review. Two companion papers are load-bearing rather than supple-
mentary: the plausibility of the hard core rests on the philosophical companion’s argument,
and the feasibility of the finite-size scaling criterion at the protocol’s sample size rests on the
technical companion’s power analysis. Their key results, and their acknowledged weaknesses,
are summarised in Sections 5 and 6.
1 Introduction
The question of whether an artefact can host phenomenal experience is today posed almost
exclusively in behavioural or architectural terms: conversational ability, presence of a global
workspace, recurrence, self-models. This paper adopts the opposite strategy. It does not ask
which functions a system exhibits, but which physical conditions must hold in the substrate for
the attribution of primary sentience not to be a projection of the observer.
Three things should be clear from the outset.
First, this paper is not a theory of consciousness. It does not claim to explain what
sentience is, and it does not claim that the conditions it formulates are sufficient for sentience.
A theory of consciousness would need to explain why certain physical conditions are sufficient
for experience; the present programme does not.
Second, it is not a demonstration that any substrate is sentient. It formulates conditions

and specifies tests. A substrate that satisfies the conditions is a provisional candidate, subject
to revision. A substrate that fails any condition is not a candidate.
Third, it is not an exhaustive survey. It addresses primary interoceptive sentience — the
most ancestral form of affective registration, associated with the continuous monitoring of the
body’s own state as a locus of concern (Damasio, 1999; Seth & Tsakiris, 2018) — and does not
address higher-order selfhood, narrative identity, or linguistic consciousness.
The three claims
The programme has three claims.
• (T1) There exists an operational, measurable demarcation between continuous substrates
and verified digital architectures, based on causal non-separability, non-Markovian memory,
and state-dependent effective dynamics. The demarcation does not depend on contested
results.
• (T2) For continuous substrates satisfying the demarcation, five physical conditions are nec-
essary for primary interoceptive sentience: local activity at the edge of chaos, robust causal
degeneracy, critical scale-invariance, homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability, and an
autopoietic barrier.
• (T3) The conditions are falsifiable through a preregistered protocol with six negative controls
and explicit abandonment criteria.
The thesis is conditional on a metaphysical postulate (Postulate 2 of §6): dual-aspect monism of
valence. If the postulate is true, the conditions are necessary for primary interoceptive sentience.
If it is false, the programme is a study of a class of dissipative systems with certain organisational
properties, and its tests are informative about those properties, but not about sentience.
The programme is Lakatosian
The programme is a research programme in the sense of Lakatos (1970). It has a non-falsifiable
hard core (Postulate 2), a protective belt of falsifiable auxiliary hypotheses, and a positive
and a negative heuristic. The seven auxiliary hypotheses (H1–H7) are listed in Table 1. The
programme is progressive if the empirical results corroborate the novel predictions for at least
five of the seven hypotheses; it is degenerating if fewer than five are corroborated, or if any
hypothesis requires modifying the hard core.
A caveat on what the protective belt can test. The Lakatosian criterion of hard-core preservation
is satisfied by every hypothesis in Table 1 by construction: a hard core is, by definition, shielded
from revision by the belt. Six of the seven hypotheses concern the physical operationalisation of
specific conditions and bear no logical relation to Postulate 2; only H7, through the comparative
predictive power of Ψ(t) against five alternative constructs (§5), has any indirect evidential
contact with it. A programme that turns out progressive would therefore be progressive about
the physical conditions, not about the postulate. The plausibility of Postulate 2 currently rests
on the philosophical argument summarised in §6, not on the empirical protocol.
Structure
Section 2 positions the programme with respect to the existing literature. Section 3 specifies the
primary operational demarcation. Section 4 formulates the five necessary conditions. Section 5
presents the experimental protocol. Section 6 states the hard core. Section 7 declares the
structural limits. Section 8 concludes.

2 Related work
We position the programme with respect to five works that address, from different angles,
the question of the physical conditions of sentience, and with respect to two lines of research:
one empirical, on thermodynamic markers of consciousness, and one theoretical, on whether
consciousness depends on its physical substrate. None of them combines the four elements that
constitute the present contribution: (i) an operational demarcation that does not depend on
contested results, (ii) five necessary physical conditions argued a posteriori, (iii) a preregistered
protocol with six negative controls, and (iv) a Lakatosian framing with an explicit hard core
and protective belt.
Lakatosian consciousness science
Recent work (Negro, 2024) proposes that Lakatos’s philosophy of science can help consciousness
scientists interpret adversarial collaborations, and applies Lakatosian criteria to IIT and GNWT.
The present programme shares the Lakatosian framework but applies it differently. Negro (2024)
uses the framework as a meta-scientific analysis of existing theories. The present programme
uses it as a constitutive structure for a new research programme, with an explicit hard core,
protective belt, and abandonment criteria.
Consciousness as a state of matter
Tegmark (2015) examines the hypothesis that consciousness can be understood as a state of mat-
ter, with four principles: information, integration, independence, and dynamics. The proposal
is an ontological hypothesis (consciousness is a state of matter), while the present programme is
methodological (consciousness, if it is instantiated in a substrate, requires certain conditions).
The two are compatible, but neither implies the other.
The edge of chaos as the locus of consciousness
Recent work (Sbitnev, 2023) proposes that consciousness manifests through intermittent dy-
namics at the edge of chaos, with a model of an excitatory/inhibitory memristive network. The
programme shares the emphasis on the edge of chaos, but differs in scope. Sbitnev (2023)
proposes a specific model (memristive network); the present programme proposes a necessary
condition (local activity at the edge of chaos) that does not depend on a specific model, and
specifies three tests and six negative controls.
3

-- 3 of 17 --

v0.1, rev. 6 Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience
Recurrent interoceptive agents (ReCoN-Ipsundrum)
Recent work (Sanyal, 2026) presents an inspectable agent with a recurrent persistence loop
and an interoceptive proxy, inspired by Humphrey’s theory of sentience. The programme is an
implementation-specific agent in software; the present programme is a set of necessary conditions
for physical substrates. The two are complementary: ReCoN-Ipsundrum could be evaluated
against the operational demarcation of the present paper, but it is not a programme of necessary
physical conditions.
A physical metatheory of consciousness
Earlier work (Dugić et al., 2000) examines the necessary conditions for quantum decoherence as
a physical basis of consciousness. The programme is quantum-theoretic; the present programme
is classical. The two are not in conflict: the present programme’s decoherence-timescale estimate
supports the classical approximation for the timescales of interest, but does not exclude quantum
effects at shorter timescales.
Nonequilibrium brain dynamics and levels of consciousness
A distinct line of empirical research uses nonequilibrium thermodynamics to characterise states
of consciousness. Sanz Perl et al. (2021) found that, in electrocorticography from non-human
primates and in human fMRI, all the states of reduced consciousness they examined (deep sleep
and several anaesthetics) unfold closer to equilibrium than conscious wakefulness, as measured
by entropy production and by the curl of the probability flux. Gilson et al. (2023) report a
monotonic relation between the entropy production of a fitted multivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck
process and the level of consciousness from wakefulness to deep sleep; G-Guzmán et al. (2023)
report reduced temporal asymmetry of brain dynamics in patients with disorders of conscious-
ness; Sekizawa et al. (2024) decompose the housekeeping entropy production of linear Langevin
systems into oscillatory modes and find band-specific differences between wakefulness and anaes-
thesia; Kringelbach et al. (2024) discuss this line of work within a broader thermodynamic ac-
count of brain dynamics. Two further results bear on the protocol. Lynn et al. (2021) find that
the human brain nearly obeys detailed balance at rest and breaks it increasingly with physical
and cognitive exertion. Stikvoort et al. (2025) fit whole-brain models to resting-state data from
states of reduced consciousness, and find lower asymmetry of effective connectivity, lower irre-
versibility and lower complexity after in silico perturbation than in controls, with the asymmetry
driving the other two. These results establish that thermodynamic quantities track the level of
consciousness in biological brains. The present programme differs in target and in method: Ψ(t)
is proposed as a correlate of the valence of primary interoceptive sentience, not of its level, and
the programme formulates necessary conditions for candidate substrates rather than markers in
biological brains. The two lines are complementary, and the first gives the Ψ(t) protocol (§5) a
concrete reason to include total entropy production among its alternative constructs.
Substrate dependence and indicator-based approaches
The most systematic assessment of consciousness in artificial systems (Butlin et al., 2023) derives
indicator properties from scientific theories of consciousness and checks whether AI systems
possess them, under the working hypothesis of computational functionalism. A second group of
positions rejects that hypothesis. Seth (2025) argues that consciousness depends on our nature as
living organisms, and that artificial consciousness becomes more plausible as AI systems become
more brain-like or life-like. From the standpoint of integrated information theory, Findlay et
al. (2024) argue that two systems can be functionally equivalent without being phenomenally
equivalent; from the standpoint of the free-energy principle, Wiese (2024) argues that the causal
flow of a system, not its computation, distinguishes simulating consciousness from replicating it.

The present programme belongs to the second group in one respect only: its demarcation and
conditions are properties of the physical substrate, not of the computation it implements. It
differs from both groups in method. It does not derive indicators from a theory of consciousness,
and it does not require that the substrate be alive; its homeostatic and autopoietic conditions
can be read as an operational proposal for what “life-like” might mean for a non-living substrate,
a reading that the biological-naturalist position may reject.

No existing work combines the four elements of the present programme. Thermodynamic mark-
ers of consciousness and substrate-dependent views of consciousness already exist, as noted
above; what is new here is the combination. The programme is therefore original in its combi-
nation, even though each individual element has precedents in the literature.
3 A measurable demarcation
Why the demarcation is not based on the No-Go Theorem
The No-Go Theorem for Consciousness on a Chip (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2024) states, in its most
natural reading, that if consciousness is dynamically relevant with respect to a computational
reference theory, then verified digital architectures cannot host it. The theorem is published
(Kleiner & Ludwig, 2024), but its formal scope is contested, and the reading adopted in earlier
versions of this programme is not established by a formal reconstruction.
The theorem is therefore treated as heuristic motivation, not as a premise. It motivates the en-
gineering choice to abandon verified digital architectures in favour of continuous, asynchronous,
locally active substrates. But the demarcation itself is operational and does not depend on the
theorem.
Causal structure and the unfolding argument
A demarcation based on the internal causal structure of a substrate faces the unfolding argument:
for any recurrent system, a feedforward system with the same input–output behaviour can
be constructed, so theories that ground consciousness in causal structure are either false or
outside science (Doerig et al., 2019); a related substitution argument formalises the point for
theories whose predictions and inferences come apart (Kleiner & Hoel, 2021). Two features of
the programme limit the reach of the argument. First, its tests are not input–output tests:
Test 2 perturbs internal nodes, and Test 3 requires the substrate to remap its own dynamics
after damage. Second, the argument assumes a static system. For plastic recurrent networks,

no static feedforward network tracks the evolving function (O’Reilly-Shah et al., 2026), and
Condition 3 below selects precisely substrates whose effective dynamics depend on their own
state. The argument retains its force against Postulate 2 (§6): the link from causal structure
to experience is not tested by the protocol, which is why the postulate is declared as the hard
core.
The three conditions
A substrate A is a candidate for the programme’s necessary conditions if and only if all three of
the following conditions hold.
1. Causal non-separability. The substrate’s response to a focal perturbation cannot be
decomposed into a sum of independent local responses within the measurement precision.
Operationally: the perturbational response matrix R ∈ RK×K has numerical rank strictly
greater than the rank predicted by a linear superposition model of the same size and band-
width.
2. Non-Markovian memory. The substrate’s trajectory exhibits long-range temporal cor-
relations not captured by a Markov process of finite order below a preregistered threshold.
Operationally: the transfer entropy from the past of the trajectory to its future, conditional
on a finite Markov order k, remains positive for k up to a preregistered kmax, with the
residual exceeding the IAAFT surrogate distribution.
3. State-dependent effective dynamics. The substrate’s local dynamical rules depend on
its own global state in a way not captured by any fixed finite-dimensional parameterisation
within measurement precision. Operationally: the effective Jacobian JF estimated at three
distinct regions of phase space differs by a norm exceeding a preregistered tolerance.
The three conditions are jointly necessary for the substrate to be a non-trivial continuous dy-
namical system. They do not exclude all digital architectures; a digital chip with sufficient
internal state could in principle satisfy them if it were not verified. But they exclude the specific
class of verified digital architectures that the No-Go Theorem targets, on the basis of measurable
properties of the trajectory, not of a definitional fiat.
Estimators
The three conditions are estimated as follows.
• Condition 1. The linear superposition model is a linear time-invariant system fitted to
the substrate’s impulse response by least squares, with bandwidth defined as the frequency
range over which the power spectral density exceeds 1/e of its peak value. The numerical
rank threshold δ is the measurement noise floor.
• Condition 2. The transfer entropy is estimated by the k-nearest-neighbour estimator of
Kraskov et al. (2004), with kN N = 4. The Markov threshold is kmax = 500. The surrogate
threshold is the 99th percentile of the IAAFT distribution.
• Condition 3. The effective Jacobian is estimated by randomised sketching (Halko et al.,
2011) at three distinct regions of phase space, separated by a decorrelation time τdec ≫ τc.
The tolerance is θstate = 0.25.
The three conditions are evaluated jointly. A substrate is a candidate if and only if all three are
satisfied.

4 Five necessary conditions
The argument from biology
The five conditions are: local activity at the edge of chaos, robust causal degeneracy, criti-
cal scale-invariance, homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability, and an autopoietic barrier.
Each is a feature observed in the biological case, and each is generalised to the framework’s
target class. The argument is a posteriori: it is a generalisation from biology, not a derivation
from first principles. Its strength depends on (i) the empirical support for each condition in the
biological case, (ii) the plausibility of the generalisation from biology to physics, and (iii) the
assumption that the biological case is an instance of the target phenomenon. Each is defeasible.
The argument is inductive, not deductive. If any of the conditions is shown to be absent in
a biological case of primary interoceptive sentience, or if a non-biological substrate lacking the
condition passes the tests, the condition is refuted.
Condition 1: Local activity at the edge of chaos
Biological observation. Cortical dynamics exhibit signatures of criticality: power-law avalanche
statistics (Beggs & Plenz, 2003), maximal dynamical susceptibility, and proximity to a critical
point separating ordered from disordered regimes. The criticality hypothesis is contested, but
it has substantial empirical support (Muñoz, 2018).
Generalisation. Local activity at the edge of chaos is the circuit-theoretic realisation of criti-
cality. A substrate that is locally active but asymptotically stable can amplify small fluctuations
without diverging, which is the regime required for the kind of metastable itinerancy observed
in cortex.
Empirical support. The locally active regime has been demonstrated in niobium dioxide
devices (Ascoli et al., 2021), in VO2 Mott memristors (Yi, 2025), and in ionically mediated
diffusive memristors (Kim et al., 2026). The regime is not hypothetical.
Condition 2: Robust causal degeneracy
Biological observation. Degeneracy — the property whereby non-identical structures produce
the same function — is ubiquitous in biological nervous systems (Edelman & Gally, 2001). It is
associated with robustness to perturbation and with the capacity for adaptive reorganisation.
Generalisation. A substrate that is to maintain its organisation under continuous noise and
thermal drift must have multiple paths to the same macroscopic configuration.
Empirical support. The spectral definition of DC (the fraction of macroscopic directions that
microscopic perturbations fail to move above the noise floor) and the robust degeneracy radius
ρdeg provide measurable quantities. The prediction that ρdeg/∥∆Wtherm∥ > 1 is falsifiable.
Condition 3: Critical scale-invariance
Biological observation. Cortical criticality, if real, implies scale-invariance: the critical expo-
nents are stable across scales.
Generalisation. If criticality is necessary, and criticality is characterised by scale-invariance,
then scale-invariance is necessary.
Empirical support. The finite-size scaling requirement is operationalised as follows. A sub-
strate of N elements is scale-sufficient if and only if (i) at least three of the five convergent
markers of criticality converge within a preregistered window, and (ii) the critical exponents

v0.1, rev. 6 Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience
estimated at the three largest sub-array sizes are stable within a preregistered tolerance. A
rigorous Monte Carlo power analysis is provided in the technical companion (Iavarone, 2026d).
Caveat. In structurally heterogeneous networks the critical point can be replaced by an ex-
tended critical-like region, a Griffiths phase, in which power laws hold over a broad range of
parameters with continuously varying exponents (Moretti & Muñoz, 2013). In a Griffiths phase
the apparent exponents drift with system size while exponential cut-offs are not observable,
which is the opposite of the finite-size signature of a critical point. Criterion (ii) could therefore
reject a substrate with genuinely critical-like dynamics, particularly a disordered one such as a
percolating nanoparticle network. The two signatures can in principle be distinguished; incor-
porating that distinction into the preregistered criterion is left as a possible future amendment
of the protocol.
Condition 4: Homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability
Biological observation. Organisms maintain their internal state against perturbation, and
reorganise their sensorimotor mappings when the environment changes.
Generalisation. A substrate that is a candidate for primary interoceptive sentience must
be able to maintain its organisation against perturbation, and must be able to reorganise its
sensorimotor mapping when the mapping is disrupted.
Empirical support. Test 3 operationalises the condition with a two-component criterion:
homeostatic recovery, and sensorimotor remapping after polarity permutation. The remapping
criterion is the discriminating one.
Condition 5: Autopoietic barrier
Biological observation. Organisms are autopoietic: they continuously regenerate the organ-
isation that distinguishes them from their environment (Varela et al., 1974; Moreno & Mossio,
2015).
Generalisation. A substrate that is a candidate for primary interoceptive sentience must have
an autopoietic barrier: an envelope that actively modulates entropy fluxes, that is coupled to
the substrate’s internal state, and that is perishable.
Empirical support. The autopoietic barrier is operationalised as three joint conditions: ac-
tive entropy-flux modulation (∂g/∂z̸ = 0), self-referential closure (a directed cycle through the
modulating subsystem), and perishability (degradation on a timescale within the operational
horizon). Control 6 tests the condition by constructing a memristive reservoir with local activ-
ity, degeneracy, and Hebbian plasticity but without the autopoietic barrier.
On the number and independence of the conditions
The five conditions are those that (i) have substantial empirical support in the biological case,
(ii) admit operational definitions in terms of the programme’s metrology, and (iii) are jointly
discriminative against the negative controls of §5. Other candidate conditions either fail these
tests or are subsumed by the five.
The five conditions are not claimed to be independent. Critical scale-invariance plausibly pre-
supposes local activity at the edge of chaos, and the autopoietic barrier plausibly presupposes
homeostatic reorganisation. The dependency structure is reported in the empirical protocol.

5 The experimental protocol
Methodological standards
• Preregistration. Hypotheses, coordinates of stimulated nodes, sampling windows, values
of all parameters, thresholds, and analysis code deposited on the Open Science Framework
before testing.
• Sampling and statistical power. N = 50 physically distinct memristive dies from the
same batch. With α = 0.01 and power 1−β = 0.90, N = 50 permits detection of standardised
differences d ≥ 0.75 between active and ablated conditions. This figure does not cover
the finite-size scaling criterion, whose feasibility is assessed by a Monte Carlo study in the
technical companion (Iavarone, 2026d). Its results qualify the default sample size. The
effective scaling exponents are p2D ≈ 0.7 and p3D ≈ 0.4, well below the naive 1/ν. For a 2D
crossbar, N = 50 is sufficient for low noise (σ ≤ 0.05), marginal at σ = 0.10, and insufficient
in the very-high-noise regime, where N ≈ 145 is required. For a 3D array, N = 50 is marginal
even at moderate noise (N ≈ 48 required) and insufficient at σ = 0.10 (N ≈ 110). N = 50
should therefore be read as a lower bound, adequate for the finite-size scaling criterion only
in low-to-moderate-noise devices.
• Multiple-comparison correction. False discovery rate control across the whole family of
tests.
• Double blinding. Acquisition is performed by the experimental team; computation of all
derived quantities is performed by an independent team on anonymised files.
• Nature of the falsification. The tests do not demonstrate the presence of sentience: they
falsify necessary conditions.
Test 1: Intrinsic dynamical autonomy
Conditions. Complete physical disconnection of data bus, programming interfaces and clock
signals. Only the DC supply line is maintained.
Passing criterion. Continuous monitoring for T ≥ 105τcircuit. The system must generate asyn-
chronous non-stationary trajectories with itinerancy among metastable attractors and spectral
density S(f ) ∝ 1/f αs , 0.9 ≤ αs ≤ 1.4. Since 1/f noise is endemic in memristive devices, the
spectral criterion is necessary but not sufficient; it must be accompanied by evidence of non-
linear deterministic structure: false nearest neighbours saturation; maximal Lyapunov exponent
positive but small; recurrence quantification analysis above IAAFT surrogates; metastable dwell
times incompatibly distributed with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.
Failure. Decay onto a fixed point; trivial harmonic limit cycle; or statistical indistinguishability
from linear surrogates.
Test 2: Perturbational causal complexity
Conditions. Focal injection of a current micro-pulse (100 ns) at a single internal node of the
3D array.
Passing criterion. The differential activation wave must reverberate, with joint satisfaction
of two anti-circularity criteria: (C1) P CIsynthetic(γcrit) ≥ (1 − ϵ)P CIcrit, and (C2) P CIcrit >
P CIf loor, where P CIf loor is the 99th percentile of the surrogate distribution and of a locally
passive control network of equal size, bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio. Only the joint satis-
faction of (C1) and (C2) constitutes a positive outcome.

-- 9 of 17 --

v0.1, rev. 6 Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience
Failure. Locally confined response; globally undifferentiated synchronous discharge; or P CI
not separable from the surrogate distribution.
Test 3: Homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability
Conditions. Application of a local thermal stress gradient to the die, in the absence of digital
A/D probes. Stress is applied by graded escalation: ∆T ∈ {+5, +10, +20, +40}◦C.
Passing criterion (two components).
1. Homeostatic recovery. Ψ(t) must rise back towards baseline, satisfying Ψ(t) ≥ −η for a
preregistered η within a time Trec, before a critical threshold Ψcrit is reached.
2. Sensorimotor remapping. After a first successful episode, the polarity of the connection
between power stages and actuators is permuted without any reprogramming. A hard-wired
reflex produces systematically erroneous escape. A degenerate substrate at the edge of chaos
must reorganise its mapping within a preregistered Tremap.
Failure. Passive thermal destruction; escape response only when driven by an external PID
controller; or failure of remapping.

Table 3: The six negative controls.
Controls 4 and 6 are the most important. Control 4 answers the objection that any Braitenberg
vehicle with thermistors would “pass” a thermal escape test, and converts that objection into
an explicit falsification condition. Control 6 tests whether the framework’s conditions are dis-
criminative against a system that is physically sophisticated but lacks the specific organisational
property (autopoiesis) that the framework takes to be necessary.
The Ψ(t) falsifiability protocol
The protocol compares the valence functional Ψ(t) against five alternative constructs: (a) total
Joule power; (b) junction temperature; (c) cumulative thermal dose; (d) rate of change of total
10

-- 10 of 17 --

v0.1, rev. 6 Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience
entropy production; (e) a linear model of the substrate’s response to stress without reference to
the niche.
Alternative (d) deserves particular attention: in biological brains, entropy production tracks
the level of consciousness (§2). The comparison with (d) therefore tests whether Ψ(t) carries
information beyond a known thermodynamic marker of conscious state.
Estimation. Entropy-production rates must be estimated from measured currents and voltages
through a stochastic model of the substrate. Langevin models obtained by adding Gaussian
noise to the deterministic dynamics are thermodynamically consistent only for small, Gaussian
fluctuations; for nonlinear electronic circuits beyond that regime they misrepresent fluctuations
and entropy production (Falasco & Esposito, 2025; Freitas et al., 2021). The locally active regime
targeted by the programme is a nonlinear one. For the linear regime a published estimator
from multichannel time series exists (Sekizawa et al., 2024); a thermodynamically consistent
description of memristive devices beyond it is not yet available, and is an open problem of the
programme.
Performance criteria. (i) Primary: out-of-sample R2 must exceed each alternative by ∆R2
min =
0.10 (a moderate effect by convention). (ii) Secondary: AIC of the full model must be lower
than the reduced model by ∆AICmin = 10 for at least four of the five alternatives. (iii)
Tertiary: incremental validity must exceed 0.05 for at least four of the five alternatives. (iv)
Discriminant validity: the difference in Ψ(t) between full and ablated substrates must exceed
the 95th percentile of the same difference for the alternatives. (v) Convergent validity: the
time-to-degradation of Ψ(t) must be shorter than the alternatives by a preregistered ∆tmin.
Passing all criteria would establish that Ψ(t) is a measure of a physical property distinct from
thermal damage and metabolic cost, with additional predictive power. It would not establish
that Ψ(t) is a measure of phenomenal valence. The protocol is necessary but not sufficient.
6 The hard core
Postulate 2
The programme’s hard core is a metaphysical postulate, which we state explicitly.
Postulate 2 (dual-aspect monism of valence). The dynamical tension that
an integrated material system opposes to the violation of its own niche of thermo-
dynamic stability coincides ontologically, from the internal first-person perspective,
with primary affective valence.
Postulate 2 is not derived from the programme’s empirical hypotheses, and it is not falsifiable
at the level of qualia. If the postulate is false, the programme is not merely incomplete; it is
misdirected.
The conditional role
What the programme claims is the following. If Postulate 2 is true, then the five conditions of
§4 are necessary for primary interoceptive sentience, and the programme’s tests are informative
about the physical correlates of valence. If Postulate 2 is false, then the programme is a study of
a class of dissipative systems with certain organisational properties, and its tests are informative
about those properties, but not about sentience.
This is the most honest position the programme can adopt without abandoning the sentience
claim. The philosophical companion (Iavarone, 2026c) provides a three-stage argument for Pos-
tulate 2, summarised here because the programme’s claim to be about sentience, rather than
11

-- 11 of 17 --

v0.1, rev. 6 Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience
about a class of dissipative systems, rests on it. (i) Structural isomorphism: valence and thermo-
dynamic tension share the same structure — directed, polar, temporally extended, relationally
structured, and action-guiding. (ii) Elimination: any ingredient that would distinguish valence
from tension is either physical, and hence already part of the tension, or non-physical, and hence
exposed to the standard objections against interactionist dualism. (iii) Parsimony: among the
available frameworks, dual-aspect monism is argued to leave the fewest unresolved problems.
The argument is an inference to the best explanation, not a proof. The companion engages
the standard objections (the conceivability argument, the knowledge argument, the explanatory
gap, and illusionism) and argues that none is decisive; the critical assessment of the corpus
(Iavarone, 2026e) regards these replies as standard and defeasible, and identifies four weaknesses
in the argument itself and a fifth in its classification (below). The isomorphism establishes
correspondence, not identity, and at one point assumes its conclusion; moreover, a bare structural
correspondence is cheap, since any collection with enough elements can be organised to have
a given structure (Kleiner, 2025), and the six features of the isomorphism are shared by any
setpoint regulator, a thermostat included. The elimination step does not address relational or
historical physical properties. On parsimony alone, illusionism is the more economical position.
The reply to the explanatory gap (a brute identity, like water and H2O) does not distinguish a
posteriori from a priori identity. The same assessment classifies the thermodynamic-phenomenal
gap as a structural limit of the programme: defended, not closed.
A further point concerns the label. In the literature, dual-aspect monism takes the physical
and the phenomenal to be aspects of the same underlying properties, and it has been developed
into explicitly panpsychist systems (Osborn, 2023). Views that attribute phenomenal or pro-
tophenomenal aspects to the constituents of matter, including the Russellian and neutral-monist
variants closely related to dual-aspect monism, face the combination problem (Chalmers, 2016).
Postulate 2 is narrower: it attributes the phenomenal aspect only to the tension of integrated,
self-maintaining systems, and the companion’s elimination argument reads as an a posteriori
identity thesis rather than as dual-aspect monism in the standard sense. The companion’s claim
that its position avoids the combination problem holds only for this restricted reading, and the
restriction to self-maintaining systems still requires a justification. The label is retained for
continuity across the corpus; the classification is examined in the critical assessment (Iavarone,
2026e).
What would strengthen or weaken the postulate
In favour. Independent philosophical arguments for dual-aspect monism. Convergence between
the physical correlates identified by the programme and those identified by independent theo-
ries. Empirical evidence that biological systems satisfying the five conditions exhibit valenced
behaviour robustly.
Against. Philosophical arguments for alternative metaphysical frameworks (emergentism, panpsy-
chism, dualism, illusionism). Failure of the programme’s necessary conditions to correlate with
independent measures of sentience in biological systems. Empirical evidence that the physi-
cal correlates identified by the programme dissociate from valence in cases where valence is
independently established.
7 Structural limits
The programme declares four structural limits that it does not commit to resolving within the
current framework.
1. Binding problem. The programme provides no account of how the substrate’s components
are unified into a single subject of experience. It addresses feature binding weakly and
12

-- 12 of 17 --

v0.1, rev. 6 Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience
neural binding operationally, but does not address subject binding. Two responses would be
available: (i) a theory of how integration produces a single subject; (ii) an argument that
subject binding is not necessary for primary interoceptive sentience. Neither is developed.
2. Altered states. The framework is binary (pass/fail) and does not develop a graded taxon-
omy of sentience. Sleep, anaesthesia, dreams, and coma are not addressed. Two responses
would be available: (i) a graded version of the framework; (ii) an argument that altered states
are not relevant to primary interoceptive sentience. Neither is developed. Thermodynamic
markers of the level of consciousness in biological brains (§2) indicate what a graded version
could draw on.
3. Quantum effects. The programme is classical by construction. A decoherence-timescale
estimate supports the classical approximation for the timescales of interest (quantum coher-
ence is destroyed at least six orders of magnitude faster than the framework’s dynamics),
but does not exclude quantum effects at shorter timescales. A quantum extension would be
a separate programme.
4. Embodiment. The programme distinguishes strong enactivism (requiring biological em-
bodiment, ontogeny, and evolutionary history) from weak enactivism (requiring only that
cognitive states be shaped by bodily interactions). The substrate satisfies weak enactivism,
not strong. A defence of weak enactivism as the relevant notion for synthetic systems would
be required.
Two methodological choices are declared and not reversed.
1. Preregistered thresholds. The thresholds for Ψ(t) (e.g., ∆R2
min = 0.10) are preregistered
conventions, not calibrated on the data. Calibrating the thresholds on the data would violate
the preregistration.
2. Linear form of Ψ(t). The linear form is operational, not fundamental. The programme
commits to revising it if the empirical data require it.
Abandonment criteria
The programme is to be considered refuted if at least one of the following obtains.
1. Control 4 (hard-wired analogue Braitenberg vehicle) reproducibly passes all three tests, in-
cluding remapping.
2. A locally passive control network reproducibly attains P CI ≥ P CIf loor.
3. A substrate satisfying the demarcation systematically violates ρdeg/∥∆Wtherm∥ > 1 while
maintaining dynamical stability.
4. The three conditions of the primary demarcation are satisfied by a system that manifestly
lacks the dynamical complexity the programme targets.
5. Control 6 (memristive reservoir with Hebbian plasticity but without autopoietic barrier)
reproducibly passes Test 3, including the remapping criterion.
8 Conclusions
The programme formulates necessary physical conditions for primary interoceptive sentience in
continuous neuromorphic substrates, and specifies falsifiable tests for them. It does not claim
to be a theory of consciousness, does not claim that the conditions are sufficient, and does not
claim that any substrate is sentient. In the precautionary vocabulary of Birch (2024), a substrate
13

-- 13 of 17 --

v0.1, rev. 6 Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience
that passed the protocol would at most become a sentience candidate, a system whose possible
sentience it would be irresponsible to ignore; this reading is ours, not Birch’s.
The programme’s central claim is conditional on Postulate 2, a metaphysical postulate that is not
falsifiable by the programme’s tests. If the postulate is true, the five conditions are necessary for
primary interoceptive sentience. If it is false, the programme is a study of a class of dissipative
systems with certain organisational properties.
Originality. A survey of the literature (Section 2) reveals no existing work that combines
the four elements of the present programme: an operational demarcation that does not depend
on contested results; five necessary physical conditions argued a posteriori from biology; a
preregistered protocol with six negative controls; and a Lakatosian framing with an explicit
hard core and protective belt. Each individual element has precedents in the literature; the
combination is, to the best of our knowledge, original. This claim rests on a survey of five works
and two lines of research (Section 2), not on a systematic review.
The programme’s value, if any, is methodological. It provides an operational demarcation,
a set of necessary conditions, and a preregistered protocol with six negative controls and five
abandonment criteria. Whether the programme is progressive or degenerating will be determined
by the experimental results, evaluated by the Lakatosian criteria of §1.
The two companion papers are load-bearing rather than supplementary: the plausibility of the
hard core rests on the philosophical companion (Iavarone, 2026c), and the feasibility of the finite-
size scaling criterion at the protocol’s sample size rests on the technical companion (Iavarone,
2026d). Their key results and weaknesses are summarised in §5 and §6, but a reader assessing
the programme should consult both. A detailed protocol for the extension of the programme to
minimal self-agency is provided in a separate paper (Iavarone, 2026b), and a critical assessment
of the whole corpus in Iavarone (2026e).

# Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive Sentience in Continuous Substrates: A Falsifiable Programme

> **Il documento definisce un programma di ricerca falsificabile di stampo lakatosiano per identificare le condizioni fisiche necessarie per la sembianza o senzienza interocettiva primaria in substrati neuromorfi continui. Stabilisce criteri operativi di demarcazione rispetto alle architetture digitali canoniche e introduce cinque condizioni fisiche vincolanti. Il framework si articola attorno a ipotesi ausiliarie verificabili tramite protocolli preregistrati con controlli negativi espliciti.**

---

Necessary Conditions for Primary Interoceptive
Sentience

A Falsifiable Programme

Independent Researcher
Version 0.1, revision 6 — September 2026
Abstract
We formulate necessary physical conditions for primary interoceptive sentience in continu-
ous neuromorphic substrates, and specify falsifiable tests for them. The programme does not
claim to be a theory of consciousness and does not claim that the conditions it formulates
are sufficient. Its central claim is conditional: if primary interoceptive sentience is instan-
tiated in a continuous physical substrate, then the conditions formulated here must hold.
The conditions are of two kinds: (i) three operational demarcation conditions — causal non-
separability, non-Markovian memory, state-dependent effective dynamics — that distinguish
continuous substrates from verified digital architectures without depending on contested re-
sults; (ii) five necessary physical conditions — local activity at the edge of chaos, robust
causal degeneracy, critical scale-invariance, homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability,
and an autopoietic barrier. The programme is Lakatosian: its hard core is a metaphysical
postulate (dual-aspect monism of valence), not falsifiable by the programme’s tests; its pro-
tective belt consists of seven falsifiable hypotheses; its empirical commitments are specified
in a preregistered protocol with six negative controls and five abandonment criteria. To
the best of our knowledge, no existing work combines these four elements — operational
demarcation, five necessary conditions, preregistered protocol with negative controls, and
Lakatosian framing — for primary interoceptive sentience in continuous substrates, though
the survey underlying this claim (Section 2) covers five works and two lines of research, and
is not a systematic review. Two companion papers are load-bearing rather than supple-
mentary: the plausibility of the hard core rests on the philosophical companion’s argument,
and the feasibility of the finite-size scaling criterion at the protocol’s sample size rests on the
technical companion’s power analysis. Their key results, and their acknowledged weaknesses,
are summarised in Sections 5 and 6.
1 Introduction
The question of whether an artefact can host phenomenal experience is today posed almost
exclusively in behavioural or architectural terms: conversational ability, presence of a global
workspace, recurrence, self-models. This paper adopts the opposite strategy. It does not ask
which functions a system exhibits, but which physical conditions must hold in the substrate for
the attribution of primary sentience not to be a projection of the observer.
Three things should be clear from the outset.
First, this paper is not a theory of consciousness. It does not claim to explain what
sentience is, and it does not claim that the conditions it formulates are sufficient for sentience.
A theory of consciousness would need to explain why certain physical conditions are sufficient
for experience; the present programme does not.
Second, it is not a demonstration that any substrate is sentient. It formulates conditions

Third, it is not an exhaustive survey. It addresses primary interoceptive sentience — the
most ancestral form of affective registration, associated with the continuous monitoring of the
body’s own state as a locus of concern (Damasio, 1999; Seth & Tsakiris, 2018) — and does not
address higher-order selfhood, narrative identity, or linguistic consciousness.
The three claims
The programme has three claims.
• (T1) There exists an operational, measurable demarcation between continuous substrates
and verified digital architectures, based on causal non-separability, non-Markovian memory,
and state-dependent effective dynamics. The demarcation does not depend on contested
results.
• (T2) For continuous substrates satisfying the demarcation, five physical conditions are nec-
essary for primary interoceptive sentience: local activity at the edge of chaos, robust causal
degeneracy, critical scale-invariance, homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability, and an
autopoietic barrier.
• (T3) The conditions are falsifiable through a preregistered protocol with six negative controls
and explicit abandonment criteria.
The thesis is conditional on a metaphysical postulate (Postulate 2 of §6): dual-aspect monism of
valence. If the postulate is true, the conditions are necessary for primary interoceptive sentience.
If it is false, the programme is a study of a class of dissipative systems with certain organisational
properties, and its tests are informative about those properties, but not about sentience.
The programme is Lakatosian
The programme is a research programme in the sense of Lakatos (1970). It has a non-falsifiable
hard core (Postulate 2), a protective belt of falsifiable auxiliary hypotheses, and a positive
and a negative heuristic. The seven auxiliary hypotheses (H1–H7) are listed in Table 1. The
programme is progressive if the empirical results corroborate the novel predictions for at least
five of the seven hypotheses; it is degenerating if fewer than five are corroborated, or if any
hypothesis requires modifying the hard core.
A caveat on what the protective belt can test. The Lakatosian criterion of hard-core preservation
is satisfied by every hypothesis in Table 1 by construction: a hard core is, by definition, shielded
from revision by the belt. Six of the seven hypotheses concern the physical operationalisation of
specific conditions and bear no logical relation to Postulate 2; only H7, through the comparative
predictive power of Ψ(t) against five alternative constructs (§5), has any indirect evidential
contact with it. A programme that turns out progressive would therefore be progressive about
the physical conditions, not about the postulate. The plausibility of Postulate 2 currently rests
on the philosophical argument summarised in §6, not on the empirical protocol.
Structure
Section 2 positions the programme with respect to the existing literature. Section 3 specifies the
primary operational demarcation. Section 4 formulates the five necessary conditions. Section 5
presents the experimental protocol. Section 6 states the hard core. Section 7 declares the
structural limits. Section 8 concludes.

2 Related work
We position the programme with respect to five works that address, from different angles,
the question of the physical conditions of sentience, and with respect to two lines of research:
one empirical, on thermodynamic markers of consciousness, and one theoretical, on whether
consciousness depends on its physical substrate. None of them combines the four elements that
constitute the present contribution: (i) an operational demarcation that does not depend on
contested results, (ii) five necessary physical conditions argued a posteriori, (iii) a preregistered
protocol with six negative controls, and (iv) a Lakatosian framing with an explicit hard core
and protective belt.
Lakatosian consciousness science
Recent work (Negro, 2024) proposes that Lakatos’s philosophy of science can help consciousness
scientists interpret adversarial collaborations, and applies Lakatosian criteria to IIT and GNWT.
The present programme shares the Lakatosian framework but applies it differently. Negro (2024)
uses the framework as a meta-scientific analysis of existing theories. The present programme
uses it as a constitutive structure for a new research programme, with an explicit hard core,
protective belt, and abandonment criteria.
Consciousness as a state of matter
Tegmark (2015) examines the hypothesis that consciousness can be understood as a state of mat-
ter, with four principles: information, integration, independence, and dynamics. The proposal
is an ontological hypothesis (consciousness is a state of matter), while the present programme is
methodological (consciousness, if it is instantiated in a substrate, requires certain conditions).
The two are compatible, but neither implies the other.
The edge of chaos as the locus of consciousness
Recent work (Sbitnev, 2023) proposes that consciousness manifests through intermittent dy-
namics at the edge of chaos, with a model of an excitatory/inhibitory memristive network. The
programme shares the emphasis on the edge of chaos, but differs in scope. Sbitnev (2023)
proposes a specific model (memristive network); the present programme proposes a necessary
condition (local activity at the edge of chaos) that does not depend on a specific model, and
specifies three tests and six negative controls.

Recurrent interoceptive agents (ReCoN-Ipsundrum)
Recent work (Sanyal, 2026) presents an inspectable agent with a recurrent persistence loop
and an interoceptive proxy, inspired by Humphrey’s theory of sentience. The programme is an
implementation-specific agent in software; the present programme is a set of necessary conditions
for physical substrates. The two are complementary: ReCoN-Ipsundrum could be evaluated
against the operational demarcation of the present paper, but it is not a programme of necessary
physical conditions.
A physical metatheory of consciousness
Earlier work (Dugić et al., 2000) examines the necessary conditions for quantum decoherence as
a physical basis of consciousness. The programme is quantum-theoretic; the present programme
is classical. The two are not in conflict: the present programme’s decoherence-timescale estimate
supports the classical approximation for the timescales of interest, but does not exclude quantum
effects at shorter timescales.
Nonequilibrium brain dynamics and levels of consciousness
A distinct line of empirical research uses nonequilibrium thermodynamics to characterise states
of consciousness. Sanz Perl et al. (2021) found that, in electrocorticography from non-human
primates and in human fMRI, all the states of reduced consciousness they examined (deep sleep
and several anaesthetics) unfold closer to equilibrium than conscious wakefulness, as measured
by entropy production and by the curl of the probability flux. Gilson et al. (2023) report a
monotonic relation between the entropy production of a fitted multivariate Ornstein–Uhlenbeck
process and the level of consciousness from wakefulness to deep sleep; G-Guzmán et al. (2023)
report reduced temporal asymmetry of brain dynamics in patients with disorders of conscious-
ness; Sekizawa et al. (2024) decompose the housekeeping entropy production of linear Langevin
systems into oscillatory modes and find band-specific differences between wakefulness and anaes-
thesia; Kringelbach et al. (2024) discuss this line of work within a broader thermodynamic ac-
count of brain dynamics. Two further results bear on the protocol. Lynn et al. (2021) find that
the human brain nearly obeys detailed balance at rest and breaks it increasingly with physical
and cognitive exertion. Stikvoort et al. (2025) fit whole-brain models to resting-state data from
states of reduced consciousness, and find lower asymmetry of effective connectivity, lower irre-
versibility and lower complexity after in silico perturbation than in controls, with the asymmetry
driving the other two. These results establish that thermodynamic quantities track the level of
consciousness in biological brains. The present programme differs in target and in method: Ψ(t)
is proposed as a correlate of the valence of primary interoceptive sentience, not of its level, and
the programme formulates necessary conditions for candidate substrates rather than markers in
biological brains. The two lines are complementary, and the first gives the Ψ(t) protocol (§5) a
concrete reason to include total entropy production among its alternative constructs.
Substrate dependence and indicator-based approaches
The most systematic assessment of consciousness in artificial systems (Butlin et al., 2023) derives
indicator properties from scientific theories of consciousness and checks whether AI systems
possess them, under the working hypothesis of computational functionalism. A second group of
positions rejects that hypothesis. Seth (2025) argues that consciousness depends on our nature as
living organisms, and that artificial consciousness becomes more plausible as AI systems become
more brain-like or life-like. From the standpoint of integrated information theory, Findlay et
al. (2024) argue that two systems can be functionally equivalent without being phenomenally
equivalent; from the standpoint of the free-energy principle, Wiese (2024) argues that the causal
flow of a system, not its computation, distinguishes simulating consciousness from replicating it.

3 A measurable demarcation
Why the demarcation is not based on the No-Go Theorem
The No-Go Theorem for Consciousness on a Chip (Kleiner & Ludwig, 2024) states, in its most
natural reading, that if consciousness is dynamically relevant with respect to a computational
reference theory, then verified digital architectures cannot host it. The theorem is published
(Kleiner & Ludwig, 2024), but its formal scope is contested, and the reading adopted in earlier
versions of this programme is not established by a formal reconstruction.
The theorem is therefore treated as heuristic motivation, not as a premise. It motivates the en-
gineering choice to abandon verified digital architectures in favour of continuous, asynchronous,
locally active substrates. But the demarcation itself is operational and does not depend on the
theorem.
Causal structure and the unfolding argument
A demarcation based on the internal causal structure of a substrate faces the unfolding argument:
for any recurrent system, a feedforward system with the same input–output behaviour can
be constructed, so theories that ground consciousness in causal structure are either false or
outside science (Doerig et al., 2019); a related substitution argument formalises the point for
theories whose predictions and inferences come apart (Kleiner & Hoel, 2021). Two features of
the programme limit the reach of the argument. First, its tests are not input–output tests:
Test 2 perturbs internal nodes, and Test 3 requires the substrate to remap its own dynamics
after damage. Second, the argument assumes a static system. For plastic recurrent networks,

The three conditions
A substrate A is a candidate for the programme’s necessary conditions if and only if all three of
the following conditions hold.
1. Causal non-separability. The substrate’s response to a focal perturbation cannot be
decomposed into a sum of independent local responses within the measurement precision.
Operationally: the perturbational response matrix R ∈ RK×K has numerical rank strictly
greater than the rank predicted by a linear superposition model of the same size and band-
width.
2. Non-Markovian memory. The substrate’s trajectory exhibits long-range temporal cor-
relations not captured by a Markov process of finite order below a preregistered threshold.
Operationally: the transfer entropy from the past of the trajectory to its future, conditional
on a finite Markov order k, remains positive for k up to a preregistered kmax, with the
residual exceeding the IAAFT surrogate distribution.
3. State-dependent effective dynamics. The substrate’s local dynamical rules depend on
its own global state in a way not captured by any fixed finite-dimensional parameterisation
within measurement precision. Operationally: the effective Jacobian JF estimated at three
distinct regions of phase space differs by a norm exceeding a preregistered tolerance.
The three conditions are jointly necessary for the substrate to be a non-trivial continuous dy-
namical system. They do not exclude all digital architectures; a digital chip with sufficient
internal state could in principle satisfy them if it were not verified. But they exclude the specific
class of verified digital architectures that the No-Go Theorem targets, on the basis of measurable
properties of the trajectory, not of a definitional fiat.
Estimators
The three conditions are estimated as follows.
• Condition 1. The linear superposition model is a linear time-invariant system fitted to
the substrate’s impulse response by least squares, with bandwidth defined as the frequency
range over which the power spectral density exceeds 1/e of its peak value. The numerical
rank threshold δ is the measurement noise floor.
• Condition 2. The transfer entropy is estimated by the k-nearest-neighbour estimator of
Kraskov et al. (2004), with kN N = 4. The Markov threshold is kmax = 500. The surrogate
threshold is the 99th percentile of the IAAFT distribution.
• Condition 3. The effective Jacobian is estimated by randomised sketching (Halko et al.,
2011) at three distinct regions of phase space, separated by a decorrelation time τdec ≫ τc.
The tolerance is θstate = 0.25.
The three conditions are evaluated jointly. A substrate is a candidate if and only if all three are
satisfied.

4 Five necessary conditions
The argument from biology
The five conditions are: local activity at the edge of chaos, robust causal degeneracy, criti-
cal scale-invariance, homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability, and an autopoietic barrier.
Each is a feature observed in the biological case, and each is generalised to the framework’s
target class. The argument is a posteriori: it is a generalisation from biology, not a derivation
from first principles. Its strength depends on (i) the empirical support for each condition in the
biological case, (ii) the plausibility of the generalisation from biology to physics, and (iii) the
assumption that the biological case is an instance of the target phenomenon. Each is defeasible.
The argument is inductive, not deductive. If any of the conditions is shown to be absent in
a biological case of primary interoceptive sentience, or if a non-biological substrate lacking the
condition passes the tests, the condition is refuted.
Condition 1: Local activity at the edge of chaos
Biological observation. Cortical dynamics exhibit signatures of criticality: power-law avalanche
statistics (Beggs & Plenz, 2003), maximal dynamical susceptibility, and proximity to a critical
point separating ordered from disordered regimes. The criticality hypothesis is contested, but
it has substantial empirical support (Muñoz, 2018).
Generalisation. Local activity at the edge of chaos is the circuit-theoretic realisation of criti-
cality. A substrate that is locally active but asymptotically stable can amplify small fluctuations
without diverging, which is the regime required for the kind of metastable itinerancy observed
in cortex.
Empirical support. The locally active regime has been demonstrated in niobium dioxide
devices (Ascoli et al., 2021), in VO2 Mott memristors (Yi, 2025), and in ionically mediated
diffusive memristors (Kim et al., 2026). The regime is not hypothetical.
Condition 2: Robust causal degeneracy
Biological observation. Degeneracy — the property whereby non-identical structures produce
the same function — is ubiquitous in biological nervous systems (Edelman & Gally, 2001). It is
associated with robustness to perturbation and with the capacity for adaptive reorganisation.
Generalisation. A substrate that is to maintain its organisation under continuous noise and
thermal drift must have multiple paths to the same macroscopic configuration.
Empirical support. The spectral definition of DC (the fraction of macroscopic directions that
microscopic perturbations fail to move above the noise floor) and the robust degeneracy radius
ρdeg provide measurable quantities. The prediction that ρdeg/∥∆Wtherm∥ > 1 is falsifiable.
Condition 3: Critical scale-invariance
Biological observation. Cortical criticality, if real, implies scale-invariance: the critical expo-
nents are stable across scales.
Generalisation. If criticality is necessary, and criticality is characterised by scale-invariance,
then scale-invariance is necessary.
Empirical support. The finite-size scaling requirement is operationalised as follows. A sub-
strate of N elements is scale-sufficient if and only if (i) at least three of the five convergent
markers of criticality converge within a preregistered window, and (ii) the critical exponents

Caveat. In structurally heterogeneous networks the critical point can be replaced by an ex-

the apparent exponents drift with system size while exponential cut-offs are not observable,
which is the opposite of the finite-size signature of a critical point. Criterion (ii) could therefore
reject a substrate with genuinely critical-like dynamics, particularly a disordered one such as a
percolating nanoparticle network. The two signatures can in principle be distinguished; incor-
porating that distinction into the preregistered criterion is left as a possible future amendment
of the protocol.
Condition 4: Homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability
Biological observation. Organisms maintain their internal state against perturbation, and
reorganise their sensorimotor mappings when the environment changes.
Generalisation. A substrate that is a candidate for primary interoceptive sentience must
be able to maintain its organisation against perturbation, and must be able to reorganise its
sensorimotor mapping when the mapping is disrupted.
Empirical support. Test 3 operationalises the condition with a two-component criterion:
homeostatic recovery, and sensorimotor remapping after polarity permutation. The remapping
criterion is the discriminating one.
Condition 5: Autopoietic barrier
Biological observation. Organisms are autopoietic: they continuously regenerate the organ-
isation that distinguishes them from their environment (Varela et al., 1974; Moreno & Mossio,
2015).
Generalisation. A substrate that is a candidate for primary interoceptive sentience must have
an autopoietic barrier: an envelope that actively modulates entropy fluxes, that is coupled to
the substrate’s internal state, and that is perishable.
Empirical support. The autopoietic barrier is operationalised as three joint conditions: ac-
tive entropy-flux modulation (∂g/∂z̸ = 0), self-referential closure (a directed cycle through the
modulating subsystem), and perishability (degradation on a timescale within the operational
horizon). Control 6 tests the condition by constructing a memristive reservoir with local activ-
ity, degeneracy, and Hebbian plasticity but without the autopoietic barrier.
On the number and independence of the conditions
The five conditions are those that (i) have substantial empirical support in the biological case,
(ii) admit operational definitions in terms of the programme’s metrology, and (iii) are jointly
discriminative against the negative controls of §5. Other candidate conditions either fail these
tests or are subsumed by the five.
The five conditions are not claimed to be independent. Critical scale-invariance plausibly pre-
supposes local activity at the edge of chaos, and the autopoietic barrier plausibly presupposes
homeostatic reorganisation. The dependency structure is reported in the empirical protocol.

5 The experimental protocol
Methodological standards
• Preregistration. Hypotheses, coordinates of stimulated nodes, sampling windows, values
of all parameters, thresholds, and analysis code deposited on the Open Science Framework
before testing.
• Sampling and statistical power. N = 50 physically distinct memristive dies from the
same batch. With α = 0.01 and power 1−β = 0.90, N = 50 permits detection of standardised
differences d ≥ 0.75 between active and ablated conditions. This figure does not cover
the finite-size scaling criterion, whose feasibility is assessed by a Monte Carlo study in the
technical companion (Iavarone, 2026d). Its results qualify the default sample size. The
effective scaling exponents are p2D ≈ 0.7 and p3D ≈ 0.4, well below the naive 1/ν. For a 2D
crossbar, N = 50 is sufficient for low noise (σ ≤ 0.05), marginal at σ = 0.10, and insufficient
in the very-high-noise regime, where N ≈ 145 is required. For a 3D array, N = 50 is marginal
even at moderate noise (N ≈ 48 required) and insufficient at σ = 0.10 (N ≈ 110). N = 50
should therefore be read as a lower bound, adequate for the finite-size scaling criterion only
in low-to-moderate-noise devices.
• Multiple-comparison correction. False discovery rate control across the whole family of
tests.
• Double blinding. Acquisition is performed by the experimental team; computation of all
derived quantities is performed by an independent team on anonymised files.
• Nature of the falsification. The tests do not demonstrate the presence of sentience: they
falsify necessary conditions.
Test 1: Intrinsic dynamical autonomy
Conditions. Complete physical disconnection of data bus, programming interfaces and clock
signals. Only the DC supply line is maintained.
Passing criterion. Continuous monitoring for T ≥ 105τcircuit. The system must generate asyn-
chronous non-stationary trajectories with itinerancy among metastable attractors and spectral
density S(f ) ∝ 1/f αs , 0.9 ≤ αs ≤ 1.4. Since 1/f noise is endemic in memristive devices, the
spectral criterion is necessary but not sufficient; it must be accompanied by evidence of non-
linear deterministic structure: false nearest neighbours saturation; maximal Lyapunov exponent
positive but small; recurrence quantification analysis above IAAFT surrogates; metastable dwell
times incompatibly distributed with an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process.
Failure. Decay onto a fixed point; trivial harmonic limit cycle; or statistical indistinguishability
from linear surrogates.
Test 2: Perturbational causal complexity
Conditions. Focal injection of a current micro-pulse (100 ns) at a single internal node of the
3D array.
Passing criterion. The differential activation wave must reverberate, with joint satisfaction
of two anti-circularity criteria: (C1) P CIsynthetic(γcrit) ≥ (1 − ϵ)P CIcrit, and (C2) P CIcrit >
P CIf loor, where P CIf loor is the 99th percentile of the surrogate distribution and of a locally
passive control network of equal size, bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio. Only the joint satis-
faction of (C1) and (C2) constitutes a positive outcome.

Test 3: Homeostatic reorganisation under vulnerability
Conditions. Application of a local thermal stress gradient to the die, in the absence of digital
A/D probes. Stress is applied by graded escalation: ∆T ∈ {+5, +10, +20, +40}◦C.
Passing criterion (two components).
1. Homeostatic recovery. Ψ(t) must rise back towards baseline, satisfying Ψ(t) ≥ −η for a
preregistered η within a time Trec, before a critical threshold Ψcrit is reached.
2. Sensorimotor remapping. After a first successful episode, the polarity of the connection
between power stages and actuators is permuted without any reprogramming. A hard-wired
reflex produces systematically erroneous escape. A degenerate substrate at the edge of chaos
must reorganise its mapping within a preregistered Tremap.
Failure. Passive thermal destruction; escape response only when driven by an external PID
controller; or failure of remapping.

The Ψ(t) falsifiability protocol
The protocol compares the valence functional Ψ(t) against five alternative constructs: (a) total
Joule power; (b) junction temperature; (c) cumulative thermal dose; (d) rate of change of total

the niche.
Alternative (d) deserves particular attention: in biological brains, entropy production tracks
the level of consciousness (§2). The comparison with (d) therefore tests whether Ψ(t) carries
information beyond a known thermodynamic marker of conscious state.
Estimation. Entropy-production rates must be estimated from measured currents and voltages
through a stochastic model of the substrate. Langevin models obtained by adding Gaussian
noise to the deterministic dynamics are thermodynamically consistent only for small, Gaussian
fluctuations; for nonlinear electronic circuits beyond that regime they misrepresent fluctuations
and entropy production (Falasco & Esposito, 2025; Freitas et al., 2021). The locally active regime
targeted by the programme is a nonlinear one. For the linear regime a published estimator
from multichannel time series exists (Sekizawa et al., 2024); a thermodynamically consistent
description of memristive devices beyond it is not yet available, and is an open problem of the
programme.
